Amid the so-called
“[ceasefire](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/02/1167043),” as imperial
grifters and [disaster capitalists](https://arabcenterdc.org/resource/trumps-
board-of-peace-rebuilding-gaza-or-remaking-the-world/) jockey to [remake
Gaza](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/27/map-shows-what-would-happen-to-
gaza-under-the-us-master-plan) in their image and in accordance with their own
interests, the genocide has not abated. In its current phase, while the
killing continues daily, its defining feature is the [deliberate
infliction](https://www.un.org/en/genocideprevention/documents/atrocity-
crimes/Doc.1_Convention%20on%20the%20Prevention%20and%20Punishment%20of%20the%20Crime%20of%20Genocide.pdf)
of conditions of life calculated to bring about the destruction of
Palestinians in Gaza, in whole or in part. From the outset, Israel has pursued
this objective through a [policy of
urbicide](https://www.thecairoreview.com/essays/urbicide-and-the-brutal-
unmaking-of-the-city-in-gaza/): the systematic annihilation of Gaza City, Khan
Yunis, Rafah, Jabaliya, Beit Hanoun, Beit Lahiya, and Deir al-Balah.

Palestinians remain steadfast in their refusal to be erased. Yet Israel’s
assault has rendered Gaza [nearly
uninhabitable](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/10/11/another-nakba-un-
expert-says-gaza-recovery-will-take-generations). This devastation cannot be
easily dismissed with antiseptic euphemisms such as “collateral damage,” a
term long employed to sanitize the mass slaughter of civilians. Intent can be
inferred from actions, and policy from sustained patterns of conduct.

Even setting aside the relentless stream of [genocidal
rhetoric](https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2024/1/14/intent-in-the-genocide-
case-against-israel-is-not-hard-to-prove), the campaign bears all the
hallmarks of design. That Israel commands one of the most [technologically
advanced](https://www.axios.com/2023/10/21/israel-military-capabilities-
explained) militaries in the world further erodes the pretense that those
killed were unintended casualties rather than the victims of deliberate
targeting, or at least a [wanton
indifference](https://brill.com/view/journals/ihls/16/2/article-p336_003.xml?language=en&srsltid=AfmBOopUDRMBzTFgJSuVIaNZEfe1yiGxts2dHeErnn2TM-6pq-u12may)
to civilian life.

Still, denial persists. U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee [recently
suggested](https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/2/22/the-carlson-huckabee-
interview-may-be-the-wake-up-call-americans-needed) that Israel has exercised
extraordinary restraint. The record tells a different story. More than [81% of
structures](https://www.un.org/unispal/document/unosat-gaza-strip-damage-
assessment-31oct25/) in Gaza are damaged or destroyed. Little has been spared:
homes, hospitals, markets, and schools. In the first [16 months
alone](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/feb/19/gaza-death-toll-higher-
than-reported-lancet-study), Israel killed at least 75,000 Palestinians,
precipitating a
[34.9-year](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736\(24\)02810-1/abstract)
collapse in life expectancy in Gaza. This is a demographic shock rivaling or
exceeding those witnessed in [Bosnia and Rwanda](https://thecritic.co.uk/how-
much-has-life-expectancy-fallen-in-gaza/). The true toll, with countless
bodies entombed beneath the rubble, [certainly
surpasses](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736\(24\)01169-3/fulltext)
the official numbers.

We have not seen such systematic urban destruction since World War II. Gaza, a
captive enclave with a besieged population that is nearly [half
children](https://www.npr.org/2023/10/19/1206479861/israel-gaza-hamas-
children-population-war-palestinians) and one of the most [densely
populated](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/10/11/what-is-gaza-strip-the-
besieged-palestinian-enclave-under-israeli-assault) places on earth, has
endured [six times](https://www.bradford.ac.uk/news/archive/2025/gaza-bombing-
equivalent-to-six-hiroshimas-says-bradford-world-affairs-expert.php) the
explosive tonnage equivalent of the Hiroshima bomb. This comparison has not
been lost on observers, from [A-bomb
survivors](https://www.democracynow.org/2024/10/11/nobel_peace_prize_nihon_hidankyo)
to [Holocaust historians](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3W5oMovARYs).

Yet Hiroshima and Nagasaki then, and Gaza today, would have been largely
unimaginable without the [firebombing of
Tokyo](https://www.britannica.com/event/Bombing-of-Tokyo) that preceded it
eighty-one years ago. On the night of March 9-10, 1945, American bombers
turned a “paper city” into a hellish inferno, incinerating some 100,000
Japanese civilians in the single most destructive air raid in history. The
attack did more than raze Tokyo; it marked the crossing of a moral Rubicon
from which the U.S. has yet to return, setting the precedent for the
normalization of the deliberate annihilation of urban centers as an acceptable
instrument of modern warfare.

**The End of the Peace and the Emergence of Air Power**

The road to Tokyo began in the
[trenches](https://stephenliddell.co.uk/2013/11/09/poetry-from-the-trenches/).
At the turn of the 20th century, war was largely conceived of as a conflict
between conventional armies. Consequently, civilians comprised [only 5
percent](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8581199/) of the dead. The
First World War marked a dramatic escalation, raising that figure to more than
15 percent of violent deaths. By World War II, civilians constituted roughly
[65 percent](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1351474/second-world-war-
civilian-military-fatalities-per-
country/?srsltid=AfmBOopohmLWXdcGEmEsFK4kZTUVFlARy6QQai27LO0G5eUlAkSIb4hr). In
Gaza today, more than [80 percent](https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-
interactive/2025/aug/21/revealed-israeli-militarys-own-data-indicates-
civilian-death-rate-of-83-in-gaza-war) of those killed are civilians.

The initial leap in destructiveness, as the mechanized mass killing of World
War I left vast swaths of the globe strewn with mutilated bodies of a [lost
generation](https://ww1hull.com/changes-in-population-after-ww1/the-legacy-of-
ww1/), produced contradictory responses. For many, the senseless slaughter
made clear that armed conflict could no longer be seen as politics by other
means. Whatever rationales states historically invoked to sanctify organized
violence collapsed, as war waged with modern technology revealed itself to all
parties as little more than industrialized [murder-
suicide](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-I/Killed-wounded-and-
missing).

In the aftermath of this carnage arose a wave of internationalist political
utopianism. The nascent [League of
Nations](https://www.britannica.com/topic/League-of-Nations) promised a forum
in which states could resolve conflicts through diplomacy. The 1925 [Geneva
Protocol](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/geneva-gas-prot-1925)
sought to ban the worst excesses of the recent war, prohibiting chemical and
biological weapons. The 1928 [Kellogg-Briand
Pact](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1921-1936/kellogg) went further,
renouncing war altogether. To many, it seemed conceivable that it truly had
been the war to end all wars.

Yet such sentiments soon yielded to geopolitical realities and to a mounting
conviction that future wars could not be prevented, only won. For a new
generation of military strategists, the stalemate of the trenches was less a
cautionary tale than a technical problem to be solved. As Italian General
[Giulio Douhet](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Giulio-Douhet) insisted,
the answer was [air
power](https://www.airuniversity.af.edu/Portals/10/AUPress/Books/B_0160_DOUHET_THE_COMMAND_OF_THE_AIR.pdf).
Bombers could fly over the front lines, shatter societies from above, and
deliver decisive victory.

The [early architects](https://www.britannica.com/event/strategic-bombing-
during-World-War-II) of aerial Armageddon sought not only the obliteration of
cities but also the erosion of the longstanding principle of [civilian
immunity](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/customary-ihl/v1/rule6). If
noncombatants could not be targeted outright, then the definition of
“civilian” had to be stretched to the point of incoherence. Military planners
justified this shift with a perverse claim that targeting civilians was the
humanitarian path, since swift, concentrated destruction would supposedly end
wars more quickly.

As U.S. Army Air Forces General Curtis LeMay [later put
it](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1995/06/19/the-general-and-world-war-
iii), in war “you’ve got to kill people, and when you’ve killed enough they
stop fighting.” Others insisted that in a total war there were in effect [no
civilians](https://digital-
commons.usnwc.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1000&context=newport-papers). If
workers contributed to the war effort, willingly or not, directly or
indirectly, they could legitimately be struck in their factories or
“[dehoused](https://www.eiu.edu/historia/2010Joyner.pdf)” in their homes.

In less crude terms, with the veneer of scientific theory to legitimize the
practice, a cadre of defense intellectuals advanced the idea that “morale,” or
the collective will to fight, could itself be treated as a target. Yet as
historian Ran Zwigenberg [makes
plain](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/N/bo197007725.html),
morale was an imprecise and nebulous concept, and merely served as “another
abstraction that allowed for the indiscriminate killing of civilians.” The
“psychological science” behind it, the claim that societies possess a breaking
point rested on little empirical evidence.

This conclusion was not borne out in Britain, where Nazi bombing [during the
Blitz](https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-11213968) failed to break resistance.
Its validity was [further
undermined](https://www.airuniversity.af.edu/Portals/10/AUPress/Books/B_0020_SPANGRUD_STRATEGIC_BOMBING_SURVEYS.pdf)
after the war by the findings of the U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey.
Ultimately, as Robert Pape concluded in [_Bombing to
Win_](https://www.cornellpress.cornell.edu/book/9780801431340/bombing-to-
win/#bookTabs=1), bombing civilians has rarely, if ever, proved decisive in
compelling governments to concede or collapse and, if anything it stiffens
resolve. In short, collective punishment against civilians succeeds only in
making war more horrific and criminal while failing to render it significantly
shorter.

**The Shattering of the Bombing Taboo**

Washington was slow to embrace this descent into unrestrained aerial warfare.
This was a practice that in the 1920s and 1930s, became increasingly
commonplace: Britain [in Iraq](https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-29441383),
Italy [in Abyssinia](https://www.zinnedproject.org/news/tdih/ethiopia-
invaded/) [and Spain](https://www.zinnedproject.org/news/tdih/bombing-of-
guernica/) alongside Nazi Germany, and Japan [in
China](https://www.britannica.com/event/Second-Sino-Japanese-War). Such
campaigns were widely condemned for what they were, a fundamental breach of
the laws of war.

Some prescient observers recognized where this trajectory would inevitably
lead. Leo Szilard, who would soon serve as a [central
catalyst](https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/key-documents/einstein-szilard-
letter/) in the development of the atomic bomb, warned even before such a
weapon was feasible that the logic of aerial bombardment pointed toward
catastrophe. “The discoveries of scientists,” [he
cautioned](https://archive.org/details/leoszilardhisver0000spen/page/n5/mode/2up),
“have given weapons to mankind which may destroy our present civilization if
we do not succeed in avoiding future wars.”

But the clearest expression of American opposition came from President
Roosevelt himself. On the first day of World War II, he called on the warring
parties to renounce the “[inhuman
barbarism](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1939v01/d564)”
that was “the bombardment from the air of civilian populations or of
unfortified cities.” Even months into the fighting, he [doubled
down](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1933-39/d612),
emphasizing that the United States has long “pursued a policy of
wholeheartedly condemning the unprovoked bombing and machine gunning of
civilian populations from the air.”

Yet with the U.S. entry into the war, Washington quickly disregarded this
prior prohibition, joining the British in bombing German industrial cities.
The campaign, justified as retaliation for [the
Blitz](https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/blitz-1940), during
which the Nazis killed 43,000 civilians, would inflict more than ten times the
fatalities. As John Gordon of the Sunday Express [wrote
approvingly](https://archive.org/details/onevoicepacifist0000brit), “Germany,
the originator of war by air terror, is now finding that terror recoiling on
herself with an intensity that even Hitler in his most sadistic dreams never
thought possible.”

Given the wartime mobilization and the existential stakes, it is perhaps
unsurprising that there was little opposition to these Allied tactics. But it
was not nonexistent. A small transatlantic coalition of pacifists and
religious leaders under the banner of the [Bombing Restriction
Committee](https://www.jstor.org/stable/43896664), issued a series of
pamphlets condemning the immorality and strategic short-sightedness of the
campaign. They warned if the Allies resorted to the tactics of the Nazis, they
risked replicating in victory the very methods they claimed to be fighting to
defeat.

Among those who called attention to the perilous precedent being set was the
American theologian, [John Ford](https://www.americamagazine.org/from-our-
archives/2014/03/18/fords-foundation/). Responding to the claim that virtually
everyone in an industrial society constituted a legitimate military target,
Ford pointed out that in an average city such as Boston at most a quarter of
the population could plausibly be said to work in war industry. The vast
majority were therefore incontrovertibly protected under international law.
“Even in the most totally war-minded country in the world,” [he
insisted](https://theahi.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/10/Ford-Morality-of-
Obliteration-Bombing.pdf), “certainly innocent civilians far outnumber those
whose status could be considered doubtful.” Phrases such as “military
necessity,” he warned, had consequently become little more than “a mere
catchword, and a cloak for every sort of excess.”

Yet the drumbeat of war drowned out dissent over the means in pursuit of the
end of the war. From generals and government officials to [Walt
Disney](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUeKeN9bXSE) and the [Looney
Tunes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sy9rGAO-qfc), air power was celebrated
across American political and cultural life. Yet the most destructive phase
was to come. It was in Japan that the U.S. would most fully embrace its
identity as a “[bombing country](https://www.maurer.ca/USBombing.html)”
(having bombed more than 30 countries since 1945).

**The Long Shadow of Tokyo**

In January 1945, [Curtis
LeMay](https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/profile/curtis-lemay/) assumed
command of the strategic air campaign against Japan. For the next eight
months, he would preside over the firebombing of [67 Japanese
cities](https://www.ditext.com/japan/napalm.html). The campaign began in force
on March 9-10, 1945, with [Operation
Meetinghouse](https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/hellfire-earth-
operation-meetinghouse). That night, 334 B-29 bombers circled the skies over
Tokyo, unleashing 1,665 tons of napalm on densely populated neighborhoods
below. Tokyo was a tinderbox. Within hours, the city [was
transformed](https://apjjf.org/2011/9/3/bret-fisk/3471/article) into a sea of
flame and, by morning, reduced to a landscape of ash.

The [napalm](https://www.coffeeordie.com/article/napalm-history), a gelatinous
petroleum-based weapon developed at Harvard in 1942, burned to death [up to
200,000](https://apjjf.org/2016/23/selden) people, by some more recent
estimates. The raid charred at least 15 square miles of the city and left more
than a million homeless. In the aftermath, the New York Times
[suggested](https://www.nytimes.com/1945/05/30/archives/51-square-miles-
burned-out-in-six-b29-attacks-on-tokyo-lemay-backs.html) that one to two
million people were killed. While a clear exaggeration, such sensationalist
reports revealed something valuable to military planners: the public had an
appetite [for merciless](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/42475/war-
without-mercy-by-john-w-dower/) violence against the “enemy.” This perception
helped give a green light not only for the continued months of bombing but
also for the atomic bombings that followed.

But despite relying on the language of military necessity, the Tokyo bombing
scarcely maintained the pretense of striking military targets. With the
military deployed to the front lines, it was women and children, the sick and
injured, and the elderly who remained behind. The aerial campaign thus
amounted to a policy of collective punishment: mass killing carried out in the
hope that it would produce favorable political outcomes. In other words, it
was a policy of [terrorism](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/terrorism).

This logic was evident in the planning itself. In 1944, the United States
began constructing model Japanese homes to test these new tactics. As a [short
film](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt9466352/) produced by the [First Motion
Picture Unit](https://www.archives.gov/files/calendar/know-your-
records/handouts-presentations/sept19-presentation.pdf) explained, Tokyo was
devastated by a [earlier
earthquake](https://www.asianstudies.org/publications/eaa/archives/the-great-
kanto-earthquake-of-1923-and-the-japanese-nation/). The city center was
rebuilt in a sturdier architectural style that stood in stark contrast to the
“sprawling, flimsy wooden paper slums” that housed “millions of Japanese
workers.” The “man-made earthquakes” that were to be unleashed by the bombers,
as the narrator promised, were never tested against replica government
buildings or industrial sites. They were only designed to set ablaze the homes
of civilians.

The planners of the raid understood the implications. As LeMay himself
[reportedly remarked](https://www.errolmorris.com/film/fow_transcript.html),
“If we’d lost the war, we’d all have been prosecuted as war criminals.” Yet at
both the [Nuremberg](https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/topics/nuremberg-
trials) and [Tokyo](https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/topics/tokyo-war-
crimes-trial) trials, where Nazi and Japanese high officials were prosecuted
for their crimes, aerial bombardment of cities was conspicuously absent from
the indictments.

Despite the hundreds of thousands killed from the air, the clear illegality of
the practice was never seriously scrutinized. [Telford
Taylor](https://www.nytimes.com/1998/05/24/nyregion/telford-taylor-who-
prosecuted-top-nazis-nuremberg-war-trials-dead-90.html), the chief American
prosecutor at Nuremberg, [acknowledged](https://www.loc.gov/item/2011525365/)
the contradiction in his final report to the War Department. Even “if the
first badly bombed cities… were suffered at the hands of the Germans,” he
wrote, the subsequent bombings “were the results not of reprisal but of
deliberate policy, and bore eloquent witness that aerial bombardment of cities
and factories has become a recognized part of modern warfare as carried on by
all nations.”

To prosecute others for methods the Allies themselves had refined would have
exposed the trials to even stronger charges of [victor’s
justice](https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/justice-radhabinod-
pal-tokyo-war-crimes-trial) and might have placed limits on the use of such
tactics in the future. Instead, the precedent was left undisturbed. In this
way, a fundamental hypocrisy was embedded in the emerging postwar legal order.
The mass killing of civilian populations from the air was not repudiated but
quietly institutionalized.

The consequences have reverberated ever since. The laying waste to German and
Japanese cities was followed by the millions killed in
[Korea](https://www.vox.com/2015/8/3/9089913/north-korea-us-war-crime) and
[Vietnam](https://theintercept.com/2025/04/30/vietnam-war-anniversary-
landmines-bombs/). In recent decades, aerial campaigns [have
claimed](https://costsofwar.watson.brown.edu/paper/human-cost-post-911-wars-
direct-war-deaths-major-war-zones) tens of thousands of lives in
[Iraq](https://theconversation.com/iraq-20-years-on-death-came-from-the-skies-
on-march-19-2003-and-the-killing-continues-to-this-day-201988),
[Afghanistan](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-55225827),
[Yemen](https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/war-yemen),
[Iran](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/tracking-deaths-iran-israel-united-
states-middle-east-9.7114340), and beyond. The rubble of Gaza today serves as
the latest horrific reminder that the central lesson of this history remains
unlearned: that might does not make right; that bombing can unleash endless
horrors in war but cannot bring peace.
